`Car_Cancellation` is 1 if the company cancelled the booking because no car was available, and 0 if it did not. About 7 in 100 bookings were cancelled. Keep that share in mind. You will set every probability below next to it.

The company knows the pickup time and the time the booking was made as soon as the booking comes in. The chunk below turns those two times into hours of notice. It also keeps the hour and the month of the pickup.

```{r}
#| label: times
# from_date is the pickup. booking_created is when the booking was made.
# Both are month/day/two-digit year, then hour:minute.
# The zone is fixed so R does not shift the clock hour.
pickup <- as.POSIXct(bookings$from_date, format = "%m/%d/%y %H:%M", tz = "UTC")
created <- as.POSIXct(bookings$booking_created, format = "%m/%d/%y %H:%M", tz = "UTC")
bookings$hours_raw <- as.numeric(difftime(pickup, created, units = "hours"))
bookings$hour <- as.integer(format(pickup, "%H"))
bookings$month <- as.integer(format(pickup, "%m"))
summary(bookings$hours_raw)
# Bookings made at or after their own pickup time.
sum(bookings$hours_raw <= 0)
sum(bookings$Car_Cancellation[bookings$hours_raw <= 0])
```

A few bookings were made at or after their own pickup time, and none of them was cancelled. They have no hours of notice, so the next chunk drops them.

The four variables in the model are known when the booking comes in.

- `channel`: phone, online (the website), or mobile (the mobile site). Phone is the baseline.
- `trip`: point to point, hourly rental, or long distance. Point to point is the baseline.
- `evening`: 1 if the pickup is between 17:00 and 20:59, and 0 otherwise.
- `hours_ahead`: hours between the booking and the pickup, counted up to 24. A booking made three days ahead counts as 24.

```{r}
#| label: build
# Drop bookings made at or after their own pickup time.
d <- bookings[bookings$hours_raw > 0, ]
d$cancel <- d$Car_Cancellation
# If both online_booking and mobile_site_booking are 0, the booking came by phone.
d$channel <- factor(
  ifelse(d$online_booking == 1, "online",
         ifelse(d$mobile_site_booking == 1, "mobile", "phone")),
  levels = c("phone", "online", "mobile")
)
# travel_type_id: 1 = long distance, 2 = point to point, 3 = hourly rental.
d$trip <- factor(
  c("long distance", "point to point", "hourly rental")[d$travel_type_id],
  levels = c("point to point", "hourly rental", "long distance")
)
d$evening <- as.integer(d$hour >= 17 & d$hour <= 20)
# Count hours of notice up to 24. A longer lead is set to 24.
# Change the 24 if you defend another rule, and say what changed in the estimates.
d$hours_ahead <- pmin(d$hours_raw, 24)
nrow(d)
mean(d$cancel)
# Share of these bookings made within 24 hours. For the rest, hours_ahead is 24.
mean(d$hours_raw <= 24)
```

From here on, the share cancelled is the one printed above, after those few bookings are dropped. Set the later numbers next to it.

```{r}
rate_by(d$cancel, d$trip)
rate_by(d$cancel, d$evening)
```

# The linear probability model

Least squares of a 0/1 outcome is the linear probability model. Each coefficient is a change in the probability. Nothing keeps the fitted value between 0 and 1.

```{r}
#| label: lpm
# lpm is the linear probability model: least squares of the 0/1 outcome.
# Same four variables as the logistic regression below.
lpm <- lm(cancel ~ channel + trip + evening + hours_ahead, data = d)
round(coef(lpm), 4)
round(range(fitted(lpm)), 4)
sum(fitted(lpm) < 0)
sum(fitted(lpm) > 1)
# Which bookings have a fitted value below 0?
table(d$channel[fitted(lpm) < 0])
table(d$trip[fitted(lpm) < 0])
table(d$evening[fitted(lpm) < 0])
round(range(d$hours_ahead[fitted(lpm) < 0]), 1)
```

# Logistic regression

Logistic regression puts a line on the log-odds of cancellation. That line is the score. Write $p$ for the probability that the booking is cancelled:

$$\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \text{score}.$$

The probability is

$$p = \frac{e^{\text{score}}}{1 + e^{\text{score}}},$$

so it stays between 0 and 1. The model below is estimated on every booking in `d`.

A coefficient is the change in the log-odds for a one-unit change in the predictor, holding the other variables fixed. The odds multiplier is e to the coefficient. It is the same for every booking. However, the change in the probability is not.

```{r}
#| label: logit
# family = binomial estimates the log-odds of cancellation.
# phone is the baseline for channel. point to point is the baseline for trip.
fit <- glm(cancel ~ channel + trip + evening + hours_ahead, data = d, family = binomial)
b <- coef(fit)
round(b, 4)
# Odds multiplier for a one-unit step. The intercept is not a multiplier, so it is dropped here.
round(exp(b[-1]), 3)
# Odds multiplier for 6 more hours of notice.
round(exp(6 * b["hours_ahead"]), 3)
# Odds and probability at the intercept.
odds0 <- unname(exp(b["(Intercept)"]))
c(odds = odds0, probability = odds0 / (1 + odds0))
```

# Two bookings

Booking A came by phone, for a point to point trip, with a pickup that is not in the evening, 12 hours ahead. Booking B came on the website, for a point to point trip, with an evening pickup, 2 hours ahead.

```{r}
#| label: two-bookings
# predict(..., type = "response") returns the probability of cancellation.
# If you added a variable in Question 1, give A and B a value for it here.
two <- data.frame(
  channel = factor(c("phone", "online"), levels = levels(d$channel)),
  trip = factor("point to point", levels = levels(d$trip)),
  evening = c(0L, 1L),
  hours_ahead = c(12, 2),
  row.names = c("A", "B")
)
two$p <- as.numeric(predict(fit, two, type = "response"))
data.frame(
  channel = two$channel,
  evening = two$evening,
  hours_ahead = two$hours_ahead,
  probability = round(two$p, 4),
  row.names = rownames(two)
)
```

<div class="hw-q">

**Question 6.** What is the probability of cancellation for booking A and for booking B? Set each one next to the share cancelled.

</div>

**WRITE YOUR ANSWER BELOW**

The marginal effect of one more hour of notice is the slope of the probability curve for that one booking. Here $p$ is the probability of cancellation for that booking, the number Question 6 asks for. It is the logistic probability at the booking's own score:

$$p = \frac{e^{\text{score}}}{1 + e^{\text{score}}}.$$

Booking A and booking B do not share a score. The channel, the evening, and the hours of notice differ, so each booking has its own $p$. Write $b$ for the coefficient on `hours_ahead`. The marginal effect at that booking is

$$\text{marginal effect of one more hour} = b \times p \times (1 - p).$$

The coefficient $b$ is the same for every booking. The factor $p(1 - p)$ is not, so the change in the probability depends on the booking. The chunk below does booking A. It also computes A's probability again after 6 more hours.

```{r}
#| label: me-a
b_hours <- coef(fit)["hours_ahead"]
p_a <- two["A", "p"]
me_a <- b_hours * p_a * (1 - p_a)
# per_6_hours_pp is the change in the probability, in percentage points, for 6 more hours.
c(per_hour = unname(me_a), per_6_hours_pp = unname(100 * 6 * me_a))
a6 <- two["A", ]
a6$hours_ahead <- a6$hours_ahead + 6
c(p_now = unname(p_a), p_after_6_hours = as.numeric(predict(fit, a6, type = "response")))
```

# Average marginal effects

The marginal effect above is for one booking. The average marginal effect is that same calculation at every booking's own probability, then averaged. Write $p_i$ for booking $i$'s probability of cancellation, from that booking's own score, and write $n$ for the number of bookings in `d`. With $b$ the coefficient on `hours_ahead`,

$$\text{AME of one more hour} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} b \times p_i \times (1 - p_i).$$

It is one number for every booking at once. Question 8 asks for 6 more hours of notice, in percentage points. That is $100 \times 6$ times the average above.

```{r}
#| label: ame-hours
# p is the probability of cancellation for each booking in d.
p <- as.numeric(predict(fit, type = "response"))
me_hours <- coef(fit)["hours_ahead"] * p * (1 - p)
c(ame_per_hour = mean(me_hours), ame_per_6_hours_pp = 100 * 6 * mean(me_hours))
```

Each booking has its own marginal effect. The red line is their average.

```{r}
#| label: me-hist
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4.2
# binwidth is only for the picture.
me_pp <- data.frame(pp = 100 * 6 * me_hours)
ggplot(me_pp, aes(pp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#182C4B", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(me_pp$pp), color = "#C41230", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Change in the probability for 6 more hours of notice (percentage points)",
    y = "Bookings",
    title = "Marginal effect of 6 more hours, one per booking"
  ) +
  theme_hw()
```

For website against phone, the step is a switch from one channel to the other, not another hour of notice. For each booking, compute the probability twice, once as a website booking and once by phone, with the trip, the evening, and the hours of notice held fixed. Question 8 asks for the average of those differences, in percentage points:

$$\frac{100}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(p_i^{\text{website}} - p_i^{\text{phone}}\right).$$

# Assessing the classification accuracy

This part uses the second half of the logistic regression class: the cut, the four cells, the ROC curve, and the lift. It asks how well the model sorts bookings it was not estimated on. Train the same model on 70% of the bookings. Use the other 30% only to test it.

```{r}
#| label: split
# Seed 46704 so the split is the same each time you knit.
set.seed(46704)
test_id <- sample(nrow(d), floor(0.30 * nrow(d)))
train <- d[-test_id, ]
test  <- d[test_id, ]
fit_train <- glm(cancel ~ channel + trip + evening + hours_ahead, data = train, family = binomial)
p_test <- predict(fit_train, test, type = "response")
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test), test_cancelled = sum(test$cancel))
range(p_test)
```

```{r}
#| label: cut-half
# Call a booking "cancel" when its probability is above 0.5.
call <- p_test > 0.5
table(call = call, cancelled = test$cancel)
# Share of test bookings called correctly.
mean(call == (test$cancel == 1))
# Share called correctly if we call every booking "not cancelled".
mean(test$cancel == 0)
```

What share of the test bookings does it call correctly, and what share would you call correctly by calling every booking "not cancelled"? The cut does not have to be 0.5. Each cut gives a share of the cancellations caught and a share of the bookings that went fine but were flagged anyway. The ROC curve draws those two shares for every cut.

```{r}
#| label: roc
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 5
cuts <- sort(unique(c(0, p_test, 1)))
roc <- data.frame(
  flagged_fine = sapply(cuts, function(k) mean(p_test[test$cancel == 0] >= k)),
  caught = sapply(cuts, function(k) mean(p_test[test$cancel == 1] >= k))
)
ggplot(roc, aes(flagged_fine, caught)) +
  geom_path(color = "#182C4B", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#6D6E71", linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Share of bookings that went fine, flagged", y = "Share of cancellations caught",
       title = "ROC curve on the test bookings") +
  theme_hw()
# Area under the curve: the probability that a cancelled booking gets a higher
# probability than a booking that went fine, both picked at random.
r <- rank(p_test)
n1 <- sum(test$cancel == 1)
n0 <- sum(test$cancel == 0)
auc <- (sum(r[test$cancel == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
auc
```

</div>

**WRITE YOUR ANSWER BELOW**

The desk cannot phone every driver. Sort the test bookings from the highest probability to the lowest, and suppose the desk checks the top 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, or 50%.

```{r}
#| label: depth
ord <- order(p_test, decreasing = TRUE)
y_sorted <- test$cancel[ord]
p_sorted <- p_test[ord]
depth <- sapply(c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50), function(s) {
  k <- round(s * length(y_sorted))
  c(share_checked = s,
    bookings_checked = k,
    probability_cut = p_sorted[k],
    cancelled_among_checked = sum(y_sorted[1:k]),
    share_cancelled_among_checked = mean(y_sorted[1:k]),
    share_of_all_cancellations_reached = sum(y_sorted[1:k]) / sum(y_sorted))
})
round(t(depth), 3)
```

The curve is the share of all test cancellations the desk reaches as it checks more bookings, from the highest probability down. The gray line is checking bookings at random.

```{r}
#| label: gains
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
gains <- data.frame(
  share_checked = seq_along(y_sorted) / length(y_sorted),
  share_reached = cumsum(y_sorted) / sum(y_sorted)
)
ggplot(gains, aes(share_checked, share_reached)) +
  geom_line(color = "#182C4B", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#6D6E71", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Share of test bookings checked", y = "Share of test cancellations reached",
       title = "Checking the bookings with the highest probability first") +
  theme_hw()
```
